summary: This note explains how the Major League Baseball draft yields few major-league players, using 1997 draft examples to show how unpredictable later rounds are. It also covers the draft's origin in 1965, its mid-season June timing, and its unusual size of 40 rounds plus compensatory picks compared with the NFL, NHL and NBA drafts.
one_line: Overview of the MLB first-year player draft, its low rate of major-league success, its June timing, and its size compared with other North American drafts.
key_facts: Only 31 of 52 first-round picks in the 1997 MLB draft eventually made a big-league appearance.
As of 2009, only 13 of the 31 1997 first-round picks who reached the majors had appeared in more than 100 games.
In the 1997 draft's sixth round, only five of the 30 players selected eventually made a big-league appearance.
Only two of the five sixth-round 1997 picks who reached the majors, Tim Hudson and Matt Wise, played more than 40 innings in the majors.
None of the 30 players selected in the 18th round of the 1997 draft ever reached the major leagues.
The 19th round produced David Eckstein, an all-star and World Series MVP.
The first amateur MLB draft was held in 1965.
Unlike most sports drafts, the MLB first-year player draft is held mid-season, in June.
Under the current collective bargaining agreement, the MLB draft lasts 40 rounds, plus compensatory picks.
The NFL draft lasts seven rounds, with a maximum of 256 selections.
The NHL entry draft lasts seven rounds and roughly 215 picks.
The NBA draft lasts only two rounds, with 60 selections.
